label: lem:firsthit
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $C_zh\ge h$, the difference
$P_{a,b}^{C_zh}(u,v)-P_{a,b}^h(u,v)$ is the probability
of hitting $C_zh$ but not $h$, and ending at $v$.
The two profiles differ only at $z$, where the height is
increased by one. So this is exactly
\[
 \mathbb{P}_{a,u}(X(y)>h(y)\text{ for all }y\in[a,b],\quad X(z)=h(z)+1,\quad X(b)=v),
\]
which is $Q_{a,z}^h(u,h(z)+1)Q_{z,b}^h(h(z)+1,v)$ by the Markov property. At an endpoint,
$Q_{z,z}^h=1_{h(z)}$ leaves $\delta_{h(z)+1}$ unchanged and gives
\eqref{eq:first-hit-endpoints}.

label: eqn:deltaWpq
title: Proof
body_md:
We check the identities by cases. 

      \emph{When $p,q>0$.}
For $z\le p$, Lemma~\ref{lem:firsthit} gives
\[
 \delta_zT_p
 =Q_{0,z}^h(\delta_{h(z)+1}\otimes \delta_{h(z)+1})Q_{z,p}^he^{-p\Delta}H_-^{-1}
 =a_z\otimes\beta_p.
\]
For $z>p$, both sides vanish. By definition of \(W_{p,q}\) in \eqref{eq:Wpq},
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:deltaWpq}
       \delta_zW_{p,q}
  =\delta_zT_q-(\delta_zT_p)^*
       +T_p^*H\delta_zT_q+(\delta_zT_p)^*HT_q+(\delta_zT_p)^*H\delta_zT_q.\\
\end{equation}
Notice that 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-jump-zero}
      (\delta_zT_p)^*H\delta_zT_q
 =\left(\sum_{u,v}a_z(u)H(u,v)a_z(v)\right)
                        \beta_p\otimes\beta_q=0.
\end{equation}
The scalar sum is absolutely convergent: the bound
$0\le a_z(u)\le e^{z\Delta}(u,h(z)+1)$ gives $\|a_z\|_1\le1$,
and $H$ has bounded entries. Exchanging $u,v$ negates the sum by
$H(v,u)=-H(u,v)$, so it is zero. The remaining terms in \eqref{eqn:deltaWpq} factor as
\[
 \begin{split}
 \delta_zW_{p,q}
 &=(I+T_p^*H)(a_z\otimes\beta_q)
       +(\beta_p\otimes a_z)(HT_q-I)=u_p\otimes\beta_q-\beta_p\otimes u_q,
 \end{split}
\]
because $(HT_q-I)^*a_z=-(I+T_q^*H)a_z=-u_q$.

\noindent
For $p<0<q$ and $-p\le z\le q$, 
\[
 \delta_zW_{p,q}=\delta_zT_{-p,q}
 =e^{-p\Delta}Q_{-p,z}^h(\delta_{h(z)+1}\otimes \delta_{h(z)+1})
                  Q_{z,q}^he^{-q\Delta}H_-^{-1}
 =u_p\otimes\beta_q.
\]
Since $\beta_p=0$, this is \eqref{eq:rank-two-W}. For \(z\) outside the
interval \([-p,q]\), $u_p=0$ and $\beta_p=0$. If $-p>q$, then for every $z$ either $z<-p$ or $z>q$,
so at least one of $u_p$ and $\beta_q$ vanishes.
Hence $u_p\otimes\beta_q=0$, in agreement with
$W_{p,q}=0$ for an empty interval. The endpoint identities in
Lemma~\ref{lem:firsthit} also cover $-p=z=q$.
For $q<0<p$, skew symmetry gives
$\delta_zW_{p,q}=-(\delta_zW_{q,p})^*=-\beta_p\otimes u_q$,
and $\beta_q=0$. If $p,q<0$, $W_{p,q}=\beta_p=\beta_q=0$.
For a nucleation at the origin, $a_0=Q_{0,0}^h\delta_{h(0)+1}=1_{h(0)}\delta_{h(0)+1}=\delta_{h(0)+1}$;
all negative-endpoint factors vanish, so the same formulas apply at
$z=0$.

label: prop:hit-generator
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $P=P_{a,b}^h$, $Q=Q_{a,b}^h$, and denote the three contributions
in \eqref{eq:hit-generator-expanded}, in their displayed order, by
$\mathsf M$ (motion), $\mathsf B$ (bulk), and $\mathsf W$ (wall).
The endpoints $a,b$ remain fixed throughout.

By our assumption on the height function \(h\) in \eqref{eqn:state-space}. There exists $a=z_0<z_1<\cdots<z_N<z_{N+1}=b$ such that \(h\) is constant $m_j$ on $(z_j,z_{j+1})$. Put
$B_j=Q_{z_{j+1}-z_j}^{(m_j)}$. The Markov property gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:plateau-product}
 Q:=Q^{h}_{a,b}= B_0\cdots B_N,\qquad P:=P^{h}_{a,b}=e^{(b-a)\Delta}-Q^{h}_{a,b}.
\end{equation}
In the following proof, we will omit the explicit dependence on \(a,b,h\). By our assumption on \(h\), $h(z_j)=\max(m_{j-1},m_j)$, and the adjacent projections
$1_{m_{j-1}}1_{m_j}=1_{\max(m_{j-1},m_j)}$ impose the no-hit restriction.
The endpoint assumptions give $m_0=h(a)$ and $m_N=h(b)$.

We first consider the deterministic shift motion $\mathsf M$. 
At $z_j$, write $m=m_{j-1}$, $n=m_j$,
$\sigma_j=\operatorname{sgn}(n-m)$,
$Q_L=B_0\cdots B_{j-1}$, and $Q_R=B_j\cdots B_N$.
Since $\partial_sQ_s^{(m)}=\Delta_mQ_s^{(m)}=Q_s^{(m)}\Delta_m$,
\[
 \partial_{z_j}Q=Q_L(\Delta_m-\Delta_n)Q_R,
 \qquad -\sigma_j\partial_{z_j}P
       =\sigma_jQ_L(\Delta_m-\Delta_n)Q_R.
\]
The compressed difference is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stack-generator-difference}
 1_m(\Delta_m-\Delta_n)1_n
 =\begin{cases}
 (1_m-1_n)\Delta1_n=\delta_n\otimes\delta_{n+1},&n>m,\\
 -1_m\Delta(1_n-1_m)=-\delta_{m+1}\otimes\delta_m,&n<m.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Using the fact that $Q_L=Q_L1_m$ and $Q_R=1_nQ_R$, both cases give
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:deterministicshift}
       M_j:=-\sigma_j\partial_{z_j}P
 =Q_L(\delta_{m+1}\otimes\delta_m+
                      \delta_n\otimes\delta_{n+1})Q_R.
\end{equation}
The first summand vanishes when $n>m$, and the second when $n<m$.
Thus $\mathsf M=\sum_{j=1}^NM_j$. The sum is
zero when $N=0$.

Now we consider the bulk nucleation. First consider a constant interval of height $m$ and length $s$.
Set $B_+=1_m\tau_+1_m$ and $B_-=1_m\tau_-1_m$.
The relations $B_+B_-=1_m$ and
$B_-B_+=1_m-\delta_{m+1}\otimes\delta_{m+1}$ imply
\[
 [\Delta_m,\nabla_m]=-[B_+,B_-]
                  =-\delta_{m+1}\otimes\delta_{m+1}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \frac{d}{dz}\bigl(Q_z^{(m)}\nabla_mQ_{s-z}^{(m)}\bigr)
 =Q_z^{(m)}[\Delta_m,\nabla_m]Q_{s-z}^{(m)}
 =-Q_z^{(m)}(\delta_{m+1}\otimes\delta_{m+1})Q_{s-z}^{(m)}.
\]
Integrating from $0$ to $s$, using $Q_0^{(m)}=1_m$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:plateau-duhamel}
 2\int_0^s Q_z^{(m)}(\delta_{m+1}\otimes\delta_{m+1})Q_{s-z}^{(m)}\,dz
 =-2[Q_s^{(m)},\nabla_m].
\end{equation}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:firsthit}, this is exactly the bulk nucleation contribution on
the interval. To express it using the full operator $\nabla$, retain the
two edges between heights $m$ and $m+1$:
\[
 [Q_s^{(m)},\nabla]=[Q_s^{(m)},\nabla_m]
 -\tfrac12Q_s^{(m)}(\delta_{m+1}\otimes\delta_m)
 -\tfrac12(\delta_m\otimes\delta_{m+1})Q_s^{(m)}.
\]
Substituting into \eqref{eq:plateau-duhamel} yields
\[
 \begin{split}
 2\int_0^s Q_z^{(m)}(\delta_{m+1}\otimes\delta_{m+1})Q_{s-z}^{(m)}\,dz
 ={}&-2[Q_s^{(m)},\nabla]-Q_s^{(m)}(\delta_{m+1}\otimes\delta_m)
 -(\delta_m\otimes\delta_{m+1})Q_s^{(m)}.
 \end{split}
\]
For the full interval, apply this formula on each constant subinterval and insert
the surrounding factors from \eqref{eq:plateau-product} and take the summation. The commutator
terms telescope:
\[
 -2\sum_{j=0}^N B_0\cdots B_{j-1}[B_j,\nabla]B_{j+1}\cdots B_N
 =-2[Q,\nabla]=2[P,\nabla],
\]
where empty products are identities and
$[e^{(b-a)\Delta},\nabla]=0$. The boundary terms are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \text{at }a:\quad&-(\delta_{m_0}\otimes\delta_{m_0+1})Q=\mathcal E_a,\\
 \text{at }b:\quad&-Q(\delta_{m_N+1}\otimes\delta_{m_N})=\mathcal E^b,\\
 \text{at }z_j:\quad&-Q_L(\delta_{m+1}\otimes\delta_m+
                       \delta_n\otimes\delta_{n+1})Q_R=-M_j.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Hence the bulk term in \eqref{eq:hit-generator-expanded} is
\[
 \mathsf B=2[P,\nabla]+\mathcal E_a+\mathcal E^b-\sum_{j=1}^NM_j.
\]
Lastly, for a nucleation at the wall, if $a>0$, creation at zero leaves the hitting interval unchanged, so
$\mathsf W=0$. If $a=0$, put $m=h(0)$ and
$q_b(v)=Q_{0,b}^h(m+1,v)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:firsthit} gives
\[
 \mathsf W=c(P_{0,b}^{C_0h}-P_{0,b}^h)
          =c\delta_{m+1}\otimes q_b=-c\tau_-\mathcal E_0,
\]
because $\mathcal E_0=-\delta_m\otimes q_b$ and
$\tau_-\delta_m=\delta_{m+1}$.

\noindent
Summing the contributions together, the internal terms cancel:
\[
 \mathsf M+\mathsf B
 =\sum_jM_j+2[P,\nabla]+\mathcal E_a+\mathcal E^b-\sum_jM_j
 =2[P,\nabla]+\mathcal E_a+\mathcal E^b.
\]
Adding $\mathsf W=0$ proves \eqref{eq:LP-interior}; adding
$\mathsf W=-c\tau_-\mathcal E_0$ when $a=0$ replaces
$\mathcal E_0$ by $(I-c\tau_-)\mathcal E_0$ and proves
\eqref{eq:LP-origin}.

label: prop:moving-endpoints
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First assume the profile has the plateau representation
\eqref{eq:plateau-product}.
Write $m_b=h(b)$. Differentiation of the last factor of
\eqref{eq:plateau-product} gives
$\partial_bQ=Q\Delta_{m_b}$. Consequently
\[
 \partial_bP-P\Delta
 =Q(\Delta-\Delta_{m_b})
 =Q(\delta_{m_b+1}\otimes\delta_{m_b})=-\mathcal E^b.
\]
In the second equality, $Q=Q1_{m_b}$ removes every row of
$\Delta-\Delta_{m_b}$ except the downward edge from $m_b+1$ to
$m_b$. Similarly, for $a>0$ and $m_a=h(a)$,
$\partial_aQ=-\Delta_{m_a}Q$, and hence
\[
 -\partial_aP-\Delta P
 =(\Delta-\Delta_{m_a})Q
 =(\delta_{m_a}\otimes\delta_{m_a+1})Q=-\mathcal E_a.
\]
The same argument applies to any constant short interval next to each
endpoint: split it off using the constrained Markov property, leaving
the rest of the profile fixed. Thus internal peaks or stacks do not
affect these endpoint identities. The ordinary chain rule gives
\eqref{eq:moving-hit-chain-rule}. The intervals in $K$ move with
physical time, whereas
\eqref{eq:LP-interior}--\eqref{eq:LP-origin} hold the endpoints fixed.

label: prop:folded-residual
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:T-origin-residual
title: Proof
body_md:
1. We first focus on the case \(p,q>0\). Recall that \(W_{p,q} = T_q-T_p^*+T_p^*HT_q\). For $b>0$ with $b'=1$, let
\[
 \qquad l:=(I-c\tau_-)\delta_{h(0)},\qquad
 o_b:=Q_{0,b}^he^{-b\Delta}H_-^{-1}(h(0)+1,\cdot).
\]
Thus $\mathcal E_0=-\delta_{h(0)}\otimes Q_{0,b}^h(h(0)+1,\cdot)$. The left endpoint is fixed;
differentiating $T_b=P_{0,b}e^{-b\Delta}H_-^{-1}$ and commuting
the free factors with $\nabla$ gives
\begin{align}
 \mathscr D T_b
 &=\bigl[\partial_bP_{0,b}-P_{0,b}\Delta
       -\mathcal L_cP_{0,b}+2[P_{0,b},\nabla]\bigr]
                         e^{-b\Delta}H_-^{-1}\notag\\
 &=\bigl[-\mathcal E^b-(I-c\tau_-)\mathcal E_0
                         -\mathcal E^b\bigr]e^{-b\Delta}H_-^{-1}
   =l\otimes o_b-2\mathcal D_b.\label{eq:T-origin-residual}
\end{align}
The first $-\mathcal E_b$ comes from endpoint differentiation
\eqref{eq:endpoint-single}; the other two terms come from subtracting
the generator identity~\eqref{eq:LP-origin}. Notice that the two \(\mathcal{E}_b\) terms have the same sign rather than cancelling each other.

The definition of $H$ gives
\[
 Hl=(I-c\tau_+)^{-1}\nabla\delta_{h(0)}
   =\tfrac12\sum_{k\ge0}c^k
                      (\delta_{h(0)-1-k}-\delta_{h(0)+1-k}),
 \qquad 1_{h(0)}Hl=-\tfrac12\delta_{h(0)+1}.
\]
Only $-\delta_{h(0)+1}/2$ is supported above $h(0)$. Using
$Q_{0,b}=1_{h(0)}Q_{0,b}$ and $P_{0,b}=e^{b\Delta}-Q_{0,b}$ gives
\[
 P_{0,b}^*Hl=e^{b\Delta}Hl-Q_{0,b}^*1_{h(0)}Hl
            =e^{b\Delta}Hl+\tfrac12 Q_{0,b}^h(h(0)+1,\cdot).
\]
The positive-weight inverse identity in \eqref{eq:inverse-domains}
gives $(H_-^{-1})^*H=-I$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:wall-dressed-column}
 \begin{split}
 (I+T_b^*H)l
 &=l+(H_-^{-1})^*e^{-b\Delta}P_{0,b}^*Hl\\
 &=l+(H_-^{-1})^*Hl+\tfrac12(H_-^{-1})^*e^{-b\Delta}\big(Q_{0,b}^h(h(0)+1,\cdot)\big)
   =\tfrac12o_b.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Since $H^*=-H$, the transposed factor satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:wall-dressed-row}
 (HT_b-I)^*l=-(I+T_b^*H)l=-\tfrac12o_b.
\end{equation}
Time differentiation, deterministic step motion, and the commutator
are derivations. Nucleation obeys
$\delta_z(AB)=(\delta_zA)B+A(\delta_zB)+(\delta_zA)(\delta_zB)$,
so $-\mathcal L_c$ contributes the additional term
\[
 -2\int_0^\infty(\delta_zT_p)^*H(\delta_zT_q)\,dz
       -c(\delta_0T_p)^*H(\delta_0T_q)=0.
\]
Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:wall-product-rule}
 \begin{split}
 \mathscr D W_{p,q}
 &=\mathscr D T_q-(\mathscr D T_p)^*
       +(\mathscr D T_p)^*HT_q+T_p^*H\mathscr D T_q\\
 &=(I+T_p^*H)\mathscr D T_q+(\mathscr D T_p)^*(HT_q-I).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Substitute \eqref{eq:T-origin-residual} into
\eqref{eq:wall-product-rule}. The two wall contributions are
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:half-spacemechanism}
       \begin{split}
 &(I+T_p^*H)(l\otimes o_q)+(o_p\otimes l)(HT_q-I)\\
 &\quad=\bigl((I+T_p^*H)l\bigr)\otimes o_q
            +o_p\otimes\bigl((HT_q-I)^*l\bigr)\\
 &\quad=\tfrac12o_p\otimes o_q-\tfrac12o_p\otimes o_q=0,
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
by \eqref{eq:wall-dressed-column}--\eqref{eq:wall-dressed-row}.
The two remaining terms are
$-2(I+T_p^*H)\mathcal D_q$ and $-2\mathcal D_p^*(HT_q-I)$,
which proves the first case of \eqref{eq:folded-residual}.

2. For $p<0<q$, assume $-p<q$ (otherwise both \(W_{p,q} =0\) and the terms in \eqref{eq:folded-residual} are also 0), we have $W_{p,q}=T_{-p,q}$. Differentiating, with $P=P_{-p,q}$, gives
\[
 \mathscr D T_{-p,q}=e^{-p\Delta}\bigl[
 \partial_{p}P+\partial_q P-\Delta P-P\Delta
          -\mathcal L_cP+2[P,\nabla]\bigr]e^{-q\Delta}H_-^{-1}.
\]
The two parts of the bracket are, respectively,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 (\partial_p P-\Delta P)+(\partial_q P-P\Delta)
     &=-\mathcal E_{-p}-\mathcal E_q,\\
 -\mathcal L_cP+2[P,\nabla]&=-\mathcal E_{-p}-\mathcal E_q,
 \end{aligned}
\]
by \eqref{eq:endpoint-single} and \eqref{eq:LP-interior}; their sum
proves the second case of \eqref{eq:folded-residual}. For $q<0<p$, use $W_{p,q}=-W_{q,p}^*$.

label: eq:residual-sandwich
title: Proof
body_md:
The kernel $R_{ij}$ is independent of $t,h$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:residual-sandwich}
 (\partial_t-\mathcal L_c)K_{ij}
 =1_{r_i}J_0\mathcal S_i^*(\mathscr D V_{ij})\mathcal S_j1_{r_j}.
\end{equation}
Here $\mathscr D$ acts entrywise. Each entry of $V_{ij}$ is a $W_{p,q}$
with $p\in\{t-x_i,t+x_i\}$ and $q\in\{t-x_j,t+x_j\}$, so
Proposition~\ref{prop:folded-residual} describes every residual.
The assumption that \((t,h)\in \mathcal{A}_{\boldsymbol{r}}\) gives $h(y)\le r_j$ for
$y\in[(x_j-t)_+,x_j+t]$.

The expansion $L_\pm=e^{2t}\sum_{k\ge0}(-2t)^k\tau_\pm^k/k!$ shows that
$L_+$ is upper triangular and $L_-$ is lower triangular.
Since $H_-^{-1}$ is lower triangular, so is $L_-H_-^{-1}$.
Consequently, for $m\le r$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:triangular-annihilation}
 \overline{1}^mL_-1_r=\overline{1}^mL_-H_-^{-1}1_r=0,\qquad
 1_rL_+\overline{1}^m=0.
\end{equation}

For $p,q>0$, Proposition~\ref{prop:folded-residual} gives
\[
 \mathscr D W_{p,q}
 =-2(I+T_p^*H)\mathcal D_q-2\mathcal D_p^*(HT_q-I).
\]
The right part of $\mathcal D_q$ (defined in  \eqref{eq:OD}) is
$(e^{-q\Delta}H_-^{-1})(h(q),\cdot)$. Multiplying the right \(S\) factor, \eqref{eq:triangular-right} turns it into
$L_-H_-^{-1}$ if $q=t-x_j$, or $L_-$ if $q=t+x_j$. So
\eqref{eq:triangular-annihilation} yields
\[
 \begin{split}
 \mathcal D_{t-x_j}S_{t,-x_j}1_{r_j}&=0\qquad(t>x_j),\\
 \mathcal D_{t+x_j}HS_{t,x_j}1_{r_j}&=0.
 \end{split}
\]
Thus the first residual term vanishes after right projection. The term contains \(\mathcal{D}_p^*\) vanishes for the same reason, after the left projection.

If $p<0<q$, then $p=t-x_i$ and the left factor is
$S_{t,-x_i}^*=S_{-t,-x_i}$. Let $q=t+x_j\text{ or }t-x_j$ .
For $a<b$, the residual is
\[
 -2e^{(x_i-t)\Delta}\mathcal E_{x_i-t} e^{-q\Delta}H_-^{-1}
 -2e^{(x_i-t)\Delta}\mathcal E^q e^{-q\Delta}H_-^{-1}.
\]
The left part of \(\mathcal{E}_{x_i-t}\) (defined in \eqref{eqn:endpointerrors}) is $\delta_{h(x_i-t)}$. By the transposition of
\eqref{eq:triangular-right}, it gives
\[
 1_{r_i}S_{-t,-x_i}e^{(x_i-t)\Delta}\delta_{h(x_i-t)}
   =1_{r_i}L_+\delta_{h(x_i-t)}=0,
\]
since $h(x_i-t)\le r_i$.
The second term has right part \(\delta_{h(q)}\); since $h(q)\le r_j$, the same argument gives \(0\). For $q<0<p$, interchange
$i,j$ and transpose: $\mathscr D W_{p,q}=-(\mathscr D W_{q,p})^*$, so the same argument shows it is \(0\).
For $p,q<0$, $W_{p,q}=0$. All entries in
\eqref{eq:residual-sandwich} therefore vanish, proving
\eqref{eq:projected}.

label: lem:FV-surplus
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:FV-surplus}
Let $E_{\rm in}$ and $E_{\rm out}$ be finite-dimensional spaces,
and let $\mathcal U$ and $\mathcal V$ be Hilbert spaces.
Suppose a bounded operator
\[
 B=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 B_{00}&B_{01}\\
 B_{10}&B_{11}
 \end{pmatrix}
 :
 E_{\rm in}\oplus\mathcal U
 \longrightarrow
 E_{\rm out}\oplus\mathcal V
\]
has a bounded invertible block $B_{11}:\mathcal U\to\mathcal V$.
Then
\[
 \dim\ker B\ge \dim E_{\rm in}-\dim E_{\rm out}.
\]
More precisely, the map
\[
 v\longmapsto
 \bigl(v,-B_{11}^{-1}B_{10}v\bigr)
\]
is an isomorphism from
$\ker(B_{00}-B_{01}B_{11}^{-1}B_{10})$ onto $\ker B$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume \((v,w)\in \ker B\). The second coordinate gives
\[
 w=-B_{11}^{-1}B_{10}v.
\]
Substitution into the first coordinate gives
\[
 (B_{00}-B_{01}B_{11}^{-1}B_{10})v=0.
\]

label: lem:FV-halfline
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:FV-halfline}
Fix $\eta\in\mathbb R$.
For $d,\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R$ and $N\in\mathbb Z$, the operator
\[
 A_N=1_Ne^{dI+\alpha\tau_++\beta\tau_-}1_N
 \quad\text{on }\mathcal H_N
\]
is invertible, with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:FV-halfline-inverse}
 A_N^{-1}
 =e^{-d}(1_Ne^{-\beta\tau_-}1_N)
         (1_Ne^{-\alpha\tau_+}1_N).
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\[
 \max\{\|A_N\|,\|A_N^{-1}\|\}
 \le e^{|d|+|\alpha|e^{-\eta}+|\beta|e^\eta},
\]
uniformly in $N$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since \(\tau_-\) preserves the support above \(N\), we can factor the operator \(A_N\) as
      \[A_N = e^{d}(1_N e^{\alpha \tau_+}1_N)(1_Ne^{\beta \tau_-}1_N).\]
Notice that for \(\tau =\tau_-\) or \(\tau = \tau_+\),
\[1_N(\alpha \tau)^k1_N = (1_N \alpha \tau1_N)^k.\]
So, \(1_N e^{\alpha \tau_{\pm}}1_N = e^{\alpha 1_N\tau_{\pm}1_N}\) and we get the inverse in \eqref{eq:FV-halfline-inverse}. For the bound, since $\|\tau_+\|_{\ell^2_\eta}=e^{-\eta}$,
$\|\tau_-\|_{\ell^2_\eta}=e^\eta$, and $1_N$ is a contraction,
\[
 \|A_N\|,\ \|A_N^{-1}\|
 \le \exp\{|d|+|\alpha|e^{-\eta}+|\beta|e^\eta\},
\]
independently of $N$.

label: eq:cut-nohit-zero
title: Proof
body_md:
For the convenience of discussion, we define
\[
 Z:=\sum_{j=k}^n Q_{y,b_j}^hL_-f_j,
 \qquad \Phi:=\sum_{j=k}^n S_{t,x_j}f_j.
\]
Every no-hit path at its starting position $y$ is strictly above
$h(y)=\ell$, so $Q_{y,b_j}^h=1_\ell Q_{y,b_j}^h$. Equation
\eqref{eq:coupled-other-first} therefore gives $Z=1_\ell Z=0$. For every
$0\le a\le y$, the constrained Markov property now gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cut-nohit-zero}
 \sum_{j=k}^nQ_{a,b_j}^hL_-f_j=Q_{a,y}^h Z=0.
\end{equation}
The identity also holds at $a=y$ and $y=0$, using
$Q_{y,y}^h=1_{h(y)}$.

Using the case $a=0$ in
\eqref{eq:cut-nohit-zero},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sum-hit-free}
 \begin{split}
 \sum_{j=k}^nT_{b_j}HS_{t,x_j}f_j
 &=\sum_{j=k}^nP_{0,b_j}^hL_-f_j=\sum_{j=k}^ne^{b_j\Delta}L_-f_j
       -\sum_{j=k}^nQ_{0,b_j}^hL_-f_j=\Phi.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Here $e^{b_j\Delta}L_-=S_{t,x_j}$, since $b_j=t+x_j$.
Also $\sum_jHS_{t,x_j}f_j=H\Phi$. For any $p>0$, expanding
the definition of $W$ therefore yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sum-mixed-collapse}
 \begin{split}
 \sum_{j=k}^nW_{p,b_j}HS_{t,x_j}f_j
 &=\sum_jT_{b_j}HS_{t,x_j}f_j
       -T_p^*\sum_jHS_{t,x_j}f_j
       +T_p^*H\sum_jT_{b_j}HS_{t,x_j}f_j\\
 &=\Phi-T_p^*H\Phi+T_p^*H\Phi=\Phi.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
The two terms involving $T_p^*H$ cancel after the common no-hit
equation has been used. No individual $T_p$ has been set to zero.

Only the plus components of $F$ are nonzero, so the entries used in \eqref{eqn:Vdef} are $W_{t-x_i,t+x_j}$ and $W_{t+x_i,t+x_j}$. Now we discuss all the cases.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{The minus components.}
The upper row of $J_0\mathcal S_i^*$ is
$(0,-HS_{-t,x_i})$. Its endpoint parameter is $b_i>0$. Equations
\eqref{eq:skew-kernel} and \eqref{eq:sum-mixed-collapse} give
\[
 \begin{split}
 [(I+K)F]_{i,-}
 &=1_{r_i}\sum_{j=k}^ne^{x_i\Delta}He^{x_j\Delta}f_j
                    -1_{r_i}HS_{-t,x_i}\Phi\\
 &=1_{r_i}\sum_{j=k}^n
       \bigl(e^{x_i\Delta}He^{x_j\Delta}
                    -HS_{-t,x_i}S_{t,x_j}\bigr)f_j=0.
 \end{split}
\]
The last equality uses commutation of the free convolution factors
and $S_{-t,x_i}S_{t,x_j}=e^{(x_i+x_j)\Delta}$. 

\smallskip\noindent\emph{The plus components for $i\le m$.}
If $t-x_i>0$, the lower row of $J_0\mathcal S_i^*$ and
\eqref{eq:sum-mixed-collapse}, with $p=t-x_i>0$, give the contribution
\[
 [\tilde{K}F]_{i,+}=-1_{r_i}S_{-t,-x_i}\Phi
       =-1_{r_i}\sum_{j=k}^ne^{(x_j-x_i)\Delta}f_j.
\]
If $t-x_i<0$, so $a_i=x_i-t\le y$, every interval $[a_i,b_j]$ with $j\ge k$ is
nonempty. Equation \eqref{eq:cut-nohit-zero} and
$P_{a_i,b_j}^h=e^{(b_j-a_i)\Delta}-Q_{a_i,b_j}^h$ instead give
\[
 \begin{split}
 [\tilde{K}F]_{i,+}=-1_{r_i}L_+\sum_{j=k}^nP_{a_i,b_j}^hL_-f_j
 &=-1_{r_i}L_+\sum_{j=k}^ne^{(b_j-a_i)\Delta}L_-f_j=-1_{r_i}\sum_{j=k}^ne^{(x_j-x_i)\Delta}f_j,
 \end{split}
\]
because $L_+e^{(b_j-a_i)\Delta}L_-=e^{(x_j-x_i)\Delta}$.
The case $a_i=0$ has been excluded by $t\ne x_i$.

In either case, the terms with $j>i$ cancel the free block
$R^{++}$, and, when $i\ge k$, the term with $j=i$ cancels the
identity applied to $f_i$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:early-residual}
 [(I+K)F]_{i,+}
       =-1_{r_i}\sum_{k\le j<i}e^{(x_j-x_i)\Delta}f_j,
       \qquad i\le m.
\end{equation}
For $i\le k$ this sum is empty. For $k<i\le m$ it is
$-(\mathscr Bf)_i$, hence zero.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{The plus components for $i>m$.}
Since $a_i>y\ge0$, we get:
\[
 [(I+K)F]_{i,+}
 =1_{r_i}\left[f_i+\sum_{j=i+1}^ne^{(x_j-x_i)\Delta}f_j
            -L_+\sum_{j=k}^nP_{a_i,b_j}^hL_-f_j\right]
 =(\mathscr Bf)_i=0.
\]
Empty intervals in this sum contribute zero by the stipulated
convention. This checks every component of $(I+K)F$.

label: eq:four-height-blocks
title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(h_* =\max(h(x):x\in[0,b_n]) \). Fix $N\ge\max\{h_*,\ell,r_k,\ldots,r_n\}$. Define the finite-dimensional spaces as:
\[
 E_{\rm in}=\bigoplus_{j=k}^n\ell^2_\eta(r_j,N],
 \qquad
 E_{\rm out}=\ell^2_\eta(l,N]
          \oplus\bigoplus_{i=k+1}^n\ell^2_\eta(r_i,N].
\]
The remaining input and output spaces are copies of
$H_N=\bigoplus_{j=k}^n\ell^2_\eta(N,\infty)$. Notice that \(\dim E_{\rm in}-\dim E_{\rm out} =l-r_k>0 \), which is the key point that we can find the null vector. Let $\mathscr B_{ij}(u,v)$ be the kernel of operator $\mathscr B$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:four-height-blocks}
 \begin{array}{ll}
 (B_{00})_{ij}=\overline{1}^{N}\mathscr B_{ij}\overline{1}^{N},
   &(B_{01})_{ij}=\overline{1}^{N}\mathscr B_{ij}1_N,\\[1mm]
 (B_{10})_{ij}=1_N\mathscr B_{ij}\overline{1}^{N},
   &(B_{11})_{ij}=1_N\mathscr B_{ij}1_N.
 \end{array}
\end{equation}
Thus
\[
 \mathscr B=\begin{pmatrix}B_{00}&B_{01}\\B_{10}&B_{11}\end{pmatrix}
 :E_{\rm in}\oplus H_N\longrightarrow E_{\rm out}\oplus H_N.
\]
\smallskip\noindent
We prove that \(B_{11}\) is invertible
once \(N\) is sufficiently large. 
Using $Q_{y,b_j}^h=e^{(b_j-y)\Delta}-P_{y,b_j}^h$ in the
first row, and separating the hitting terms in the other rows,
gives the exact decomposition
\begin{equation}\label{eq:high-block-decomposition}
 B_{11}=D_N-C_N.
\end{equation}
where the \(D_N\) part consists of the free random walk part:
\[
 (D_N)_{ij}:=
 \begin{cases}
  1_Ne^{2t\nabla+(x_j-y)\Delta}1_N,
       &i=0,\\
  1_Ne^{(x_j-x_i)\Delta}1_N,
       &k<i\le m,\ j<i,\\
  1_Ne^{(x_j-x_i)\Delta}1_N,
       &m<i\le n,\ j\ge i,\\
  0,&\text{otherwise},
 \end{cases}
\]
and \(C_N\) consists of all the hitting contributions:
\[
 (C_N)_{ij}:=
 \begin{cases}
  1_NP_{y,b_j}^hL_-1_N,&i=0,\\
  0,&k<i\le m,\\
  1_NL_+P_{a_i,b_j}^hL_-1_N,&m<i\le n.
 \end{cases}
\]
As before, an empty hitting interval contributes zero. We will show \(D_N\) is invertible with inverse being uniformly bounded, and \(C_N\) is small.

First, order the columns and rows of $D_N$ as
\[
 \begin{array}{ll}
 \text{columns:}&
 k,\ldots,m-1,\quad n,\ldots,m+1,\quad m,\\
 \text{rows:}&
 k+1,\ldots,m,\quad n,\ldots,m+1,\quad 0,
 \end{array}
\]
In this order $D_N$ is lower block
triangular, with diagonal blocks
\[
 \begin{gathered}
  1_Ne^{(x_{i-1}-x_i)\Delta}1_N
       \quad(k<i\le m),\qquad I\quad(m<i\le n),\qquad
  1_Ne^{2t\nabla+(x_m-y)\Delta}1_N.
 \end{gathered}
\]
Indeed, the first group of rows successively determines
$f_k,\ldots,f_{m-1}$, the second group determines
$f_n,\ldots,f_{m+1}$ in reverse order, and the last row
determines $f_m$.

 Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:FV-halfline} for the diagonal terms and \eqref{eq:free-tail} for the off-diagonal free blocks, we have
\[
 \sup_N\|D_N^{-1}\|<\infty.
\]

Next, the hitting correction tends to zero in operator norm.
The cumulative hitting bound in Lemma~\ref{lem:tails}, together
with the triangularity of $L_\pm$, gives, for every $\lambda>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:auxiliary-correction-tail}
 |(C_N)_{ij}(u,v)|
 \le C_\lambda e^{-\lambda(u+v-2h_*)},
 \qquad u,v>N,
\end{equation}
with $C_\lambda$ independent of $N$. Choose $\lambda>\eta$.
Summing the absolute entries over the finitely many blocks gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|C_N\|
 &\le
 \sum_{i,j}\sum_{u,v>N}
       e^{\eta(u-v)}|(C_N)_{ij}(u,v)|\le
 C_{\lambda,\eta}e^{-2\lambda(N-h_*)}
 \longrightarrow0.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus, \(B_{11}\) is invertible. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:FV-surplus} and using the fact that \(\dim E_{\rm in}-\dim E_{\rm out} =l-r_k>0 \), we obtain \eqref{eq:auxiliary-null-dimension}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $I_L=\{1,\ldots,k\}$ and $I_R=\{k+1,\ldots,n\}$, with
$x_{k+1}-x_k>2t$, and first suppose that $t\ne x_j$ for every
$j$. Choose finitely many basepoints $(i,u)$ and retain both
components $(i,u,-)$ and $(i,u,+)$ at each chosen basepoint.
This gives a paired finite principal restriction of $J+JK$.

We first identify the zero blocks that determine its possible
Pfaffian pairings. For $i\in I_R$, the gap assumption gives
\[
 x_i>x_k+2t\ge2t,
 \qquad t-x_i<0.
\]
For every observation $j$, the folded-kernel definition therefore
implies
\[
 W_{t-x_i,t-x_j}
 =
 \begin{cases}
  0,&x_j>t,\\
  T_{x_i-t,t-x_j}=0,&x_j<t.
 \end{cases}
\]
In the second case, the interval is empty because
$x_i-t>t\ge t-x_j$. So \( (J+JK)^{--}_{ij}=
 0, i\in I_R, 1\le j\le n.\)

Next, if $i\in I_R$ and $j\in I_L$, then \( i>j, x_i-t>x_j+t.\)
Thus, $W_{t-x_i,t+x_j}=T_{x_i-t,t+x_j}=0$. Since the contribution from kernel \(R\) is also \(0\), we have \( (J+JK)^{-+}_{ij}=0\). Consequently, every nonzero pairing in the Pfaffian series expansion consists
entirely of pairs within the left group and pairs within the
right group.

Reordering the entries in the Pfaffian indexed by \(i,j\in I_R\), it has the form
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}0&B\\-B^*&C\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 B=I+[K^{++}_{ij}]_{i,j\in I_R}.
\]
If \(|I_R|=q\), its Pfaffian is
$(-1)^{q(q-1)/2}\det B$. The same reordering gives that sign for
$J$, so the normalized factor is $\det B$, independently of $C$.

When \(x_i>t\) for all \(i\), \((J+JK)_{ij}^{--}= 0\) for all \(1\le i,j\le n\). Thus the same argument gives $\widehat F(t,h;I)=D(t,h;I)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
If $h(x_k)>r_k$ for some $k$, then
\[
 r_0(t,x_k;h)\ge h(x_k)>r_k \text{ for all } t>0.
\]
Theorem~\ref{thm:FV} gives $\widehat F_n(t,h)=0$. Thus, now we suppose that $h(x_j)\le r_j$ for every
$j$.

Upper semicontinuity and the discreteness of the heights allow
us to choose $t_0>0$ such that
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 t_0<x_j\quad\text{whenever }x_j>0,\qquad
 2t_0<x_{j+1}-x_j,\\
 h(y)\le r_j
 \quad\text{for }y\in[(x_j-t_0)\vee0,x_j+t_0],
 \qquad 1\le j\le n.
 \end{gathered}
\]
Thus, for $0<t<t_0$, all \([x_i-t,x_i+t]\) are disjoint.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:cluster}, we get
\begin{equation}\label{eq:small-time-factorization}
 \widehat F_n(t,h)
 =
 \operatorname{Pf}(J_0+J_0 K_{11})\prod_{j=2}^n
 \det(I+K_{jj}^{++})
\end{equation}
If \(x_1>0\), the first Pfaffian has the same form as other factors; if \(x_1=0\), it needs a separate discussion.

For each determinant factor, 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:initial-singleton-det}
      \det(I+K_{jj}^{++})=\det(I-1_{r_j}L_+P_{x_j-t,x_j+t}^hL_-1_{r_j}).
\end{equation}
As \(t\downarrow 0\), using the upper semicontinuity of $h$ at $x_j$ we have
\[
 P_{x_j-t,x_j+t}^h(u,v)
 \longrightarrow
 \mathbf1_{\{u=v\le h(x_j)\}}.
\]
Since $L_\pm(t)\to I$, we have the pointwise limit
\[
 1_{r_j}L_+P_{x_j-t,x_j+t}^hL_-1_{r_j}
 \longrightarrow
 1_{r_j}\overline1^{h(x_j)}1_{r_j}=0.
\]
To pass to trace norm, the estimate \eqref{eq:direct-tail} bounds
the absolute entries by
\[
 C_\lambda e^{-\lambda(u+v)},
 \qquad u,v>r_j,
\]
uniformly for $0<t<t_0$. This bound is summable over \((r_j,\infty)\). Dominated convergence gives
\[
 \left\|
 1_{r_j}L_+P_{x_j-t,x_j+t}^hL_-1_{r_j}
 \right\|_1\longrightarrow0.
\]
Continuity of the Fredholm determinant in
\eqref{eq:initial-singleton-det} shows that every factor with
$x_j>0$ tends to $1$.

It remains to consider the case $x_1=0$. Notice that the four entries in \(V_{11}\), defined in \eqref{eqn:Vdef}, are all \(W_{t,t}\). Thus,
\[
 P_{0,t}^h(u,v)
 \longrightarrow
 \mathbf1_{\{u=v\le h(0)\}}.
\]
Using the operators \(L_-,H_{-}^{-1}\) and their support properties, when \(h(0)\leq r_1\)
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 P_{0,t}^hL_-1_{r_1}
 &\longrightarrow
 \overline1^{h(0)}1_{r_1}=0,\\
 P_{0,t}^hL_-H_-^{-1}1_{r_1}
 &\longrightarrow
 \overline1^{h(0)}H_-^{-1}1_{r_1}=0.
 \end{aligned}
\]

Every term of \(\tilde{K}_{11}\) contains
one of these factors or its transpose, as displayed in
\eqref{eq:FG-terms}. The common projection $1_{r_1}$ and proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:trace-class} justify the limits
through the internal sums and give
\[
 \left\|
 \mathcal M_1J_0\widetilde K_{11}(t,h)\mathcal M_1
 \right\|_1\longrightarrow0.
\]
The remaining part of the kernel is \(J_0R_{11}
 =
 \begin{pmatrix}
  0&0\\
  0&-1_{r_1}H1_{r_1}
 \end{pmatrix}.\)
By trace-norm continuity, the Fredholm Pfaffian \(\operatorname{Pf}(J_0+J_0 K_{11})\) goes to $1$. 

All factors in \eqref{eq:small-time-factorization} thus tend
to $1$ when $h(x_j)\le r_j$ for every $j$. Together with the
forbidden case treated at the beginning, this proves
\eqref{eq:init-result}.

body_md:
First suppose $t>0$ and $t\ne x_j$ for every $j$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:FV} gives zero outside the allowed set \(\mathcal{A}_{\boldsymbol{r}}\).
For an allowed \(h\), apply Lemma~\ref{lem:cluster} whenever there exists \(x_k\) such that \(x_{k+1}-x_k>2t\). So we get 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:Fhatfactor}
      \widehat F_n(t,h)=\widehat F(t,h;I_L)\prod_{k}D(t,h;I_k).
\end{equation}
where \(I_k\) is the index set for each group. 

Let $r_{\max}=\max_j r_j$. Proposition~\ref{prop:trace-class}, with ceiling \(h_* =r_{\max}\), bounds the
trace norm of the kernel in the first Pfaffian.
For each Fredholm determinant factors, the bounds \eqref{eq:direct-tail} and 
\eqref{eq:free-heat-sum} provide the trace norm bounds as well. Notice that only heights on these hitting
intervals enter the estimates, and these heights are bounded by \(r_{\max}\), and heights in the gaps between groups are unrestricted, thus the bound is uniform in \(h\).

Since there are at most \(n\) factors in \eqref{eqn:Fhatfactor}, we let $C_*$  be the same bound for the kernels in each factor. The inequalities
$|\operatorname{Pf}(J+A)|\le e^{\|A\|_1/2}$ and
$|\det(I+D)|\le e^{\|D\|_1}$ give
\[
 |\widehat F_n(t,h)|\le e^{nC_*}.
\]
If $t=x_j>0$, we have the same bound by taking a right limit of \(t\). Finally, Proposition~\ref{thm:initial} gives
$|\widehat F_n(0,h)|\le1$. This proves \eqref{eq:uniform-F}.

Let $S_1$ and $Z_1$ be the first nucleation time and location. Their law is
\[
 \mathbb P(S_1>t)=e^{-\lambda_Bt},\qquad
 \mathbb P(S_1\in ds,Z_1\in dz)=e^{-\lambda_Bs}\,ds\,\mu_B(dz).
\]
Conditional on this time and location, the remaining marks give the same
process started from
$C_z\phi_s^B h$. This proves \eqref{eq:mild}. The expectation is
bounded by $\|f\|_\infty$ and Borel, since the graphical construction
is a finite composition of Borel maps conditional on finitely many
marks.

For uniqueness, let $D$ be the difference of two bounded solutions
with the same $f$, and put
$\|D\|_T=\sup_{0\le t\le T,\,h\in\widehat{\mathcal X}_B}|D(t,h)|$.
Subtracting their equations gives
\[
 |D(t,h)|\le\|D\|_T\int_0^t\lambda_Be^{-\lambda_Bs}\,ds
            =(1-e^{-\lambda_Bt})\|D\|_T.
\]
Hence $\|D\|_T\le(1-e^{-\lambda_BT})\|D\|_T$, so $D=0$.

Let $0\le c<1$, and let $h\in\widehat{\mathcal X}_{\mathrm{fin}}$.

\smallskip\noindent
Fix $t>0$ with $(t,h)\in\mathcal A_{\boldsymbol r}$, and consider
the one parameter family
\[
 s\longmapsto (t-s,\phi_s h),\qquad 0\le s<t.
\]
Let $s_0\in[0,t)$ be an isolated exceptional time of this
curve, meaning that \((t-s_0,\phi_{s_0} h)\notin\mathcal R_{\boldsymbol x}\)
\[
 (t-s,\phi_s h)\in\mathcal R_{\boldsymbol x}
 \quad\text{for all }s\ne s_0\text{ sufficiently close to }s_0.
\]
Then the candidate matches continuously across $s_0$:
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:shiftcontinuity}
       \lim_{s\to s_0}\widehat F_n(t-s,\phi_s h)
 =
 \widehat F_n(t-s_0,\phi_{s_0}h).
\end{equation}
At $s_0=0$, the limit is taken from the right. Furthermore, for \(h\in \widehat{\mathcal X}_{\mathrm{fin}}, t>0\),
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:rightcontinuity}
       \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}
 \widehat F_n(t+\varepsilon,h)=\widehat F_n(t,h),\qquad  \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}
 \widehat F_n(\varepsilon,h)
 =
 \prod_{j=1}^n\mathbf1_{\{h(x_j)\le r_j\}}.

title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove \eqref{eqn:shiftcontinuity}. We discuss the three scenarios for the exceptional time.

\smallskip\noindent
\emph{1. Collisions, wall absorption, and initial peaks.}
For a constant part of height $q$ whose width $\delta$ tends to zero,
\[
 Q_\delta^{(q)}\longrightarrow1_q,\qquad
 1_pQ_\delta^{(q)}1_r
 \longrightarrow1_{\max(p,q,r)}\quad  \text{ in operator norm.}
\]


Consequently, when a valley disappears, the limiting no-hit
product kernel (the one in \eqref{eq:plateau-product}) is exactly the restrictions of the limiting
profile. When $s\downarrow0$ and an island shrinks back to an
initial isolated peak, its height restriction remains at that
point. At the wall, the analysis is the same.

\smallskip\noindent
\emph{2. Contacts with hitting endpoints.}
All kernels in this step are evaluated at the profile $g=\phi_s h$. For $0\le a<b$, let $Q_{a,b^-}^g$ and
$Q_{a^+,b}^g$ denote the no-hit kernels on $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$. $P_{a,b^-}^g$ and
$P_{a^+,b}^g$ are defined analogously.
 
Upper semicontinuity gives $g(b)\ge g(b^-)$ and $g(a)\ge g(a^+)$.
Since
\[
 Q_{a,b}^g=Q_{a,b^-}^g1_{g(b)}
         =1_{g(a)}Q_{a^+,b}^g,
\]
inserting an omitted endpoint restriction gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:endpoint-captures}
 \begin{split}
 P_{a,b}^g-P_{a,b^-}^g
 &=\sum_{g(b^-)<v\le g(b)}
       Q_{a,b^-}^g(\cdot,v)\otimes\delta_v,\\
 P_{a,b}^g-P_{a^+,b}^g
 &=\sum_{g(a^+)<v\le g(a)}
       \delta_v\otimes Q_{a^+,b}^g(v,\cdot).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
These are precisely the possible discrepancies when a
step meets a hitting endpoint: one can hit exactly at the endpoint. 

For a right endpoint belonging to column $j$,
the assumption that \(g\in \mathcal{A}_{\boldsymbol{r}}\) gives $g(b)\le r_j$. It is followed by the kernel
$L_-$ or $L_-H_-^{-1}$, so the column vanishes because:
\[
 \overline1^{g(b)}L_-1_{r_j}=0,\qquad
 \overline1^{g(b)}L_-H_-^{-1}1_{r_j}=0.
\]
The discussion for the left endpoint is the same.

The cancellation also holds for \(W_{p,q}\). Indeed, the exact difference of
$W_{p,q}=T_q-T_p^*+T_p^*HT_q$ is
\[
 \delta W_{p,q}
 =(I+T_p^*H)\delta T_q
 +(\delta T_p)^*(HT_q-I)
 +(\delta T_p)^*H\delta T_q.
\]
After putting the \(\mathcal{S}_j\) matrix in \eqref{eqn:Vdef} around it, the first term contains the
annihilated right factor, the second contains the annihilated left
factor, and the third contains both. 

Thus endpoint contacts will not change the limiting kernel.

\smallskip\noindent
\emph{3. Changes of kernel \(W_{p,q}\).}
First suppose a hitting interval collapses to a positive
point $a$. The closed-interval convention gives
\[
 P_{a,a}^g=\overline1^{g(a)},\qquad
 T_{a,a}
 =e^{a\Delta}\overline1^{g(a)}
      e^{-a\Delta}H_-^{-1},
\]
whereas an empty interval contributes zero. The term \(T_{a,a}\) always comes with the correct front factor so that it becomes
\[
 1_{r_i}L_+\overline1^{g(a)}e^{-a\Delta}H_-^{-1}=0.
\]
Hence the singleton and empty
formulas match after projection. This treats the exceptional
times $2\tau=|x_i-x_j|$ and $2\tau=x_i+x_j$ whenever the
collapsed point is positive.

It remains to match across a zero signed endpoint,
$\tau=x_i$. Put
\[
 m=g(0),\qquad T_0=\overline1^mH_-^{-1}.
\]
For $q>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:411}
       \begin{split}
 W_{0+,q}-W_{0-,q}
 =(P_{0,q}^g-P_{0^+,q}^g)e^{-q\Delta}H_-^{-1}+T_0^*(HT_q-I).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
The first term is zero when there is no excess wall height.
Otherwise its left factor is supported on heights at most
$m$, by \eqref{eq:endpoint-captures}.

This change can only happen at the minus component of
observation $i$. Allowedness gives $m\le r_i$, and
$\tau=x_i$ gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 1_{r_i}S_{-\tau,-x_i}\overline1^m
 &=1_{r_i}L_+\overline1^m=0,\\
 T_0S_{\tau,-x_i}1_{r_i}
 &=\overline1^mL_-H_-^{-1}1_{r_i}=0.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The first identity kills the first term in \eqref{eqn:411}; the second kills the second term in \eqref{eqn:411}.

If the other argument is strictly negative, the mixed
interval is empty near the crossing. If both arguments
vanish, the additional expression is
\[
 T_0-T_0^*+T_0^*HT_0,
\]
and the same projections annihilate all three terms.
An approaching mixed interval is either empty or has limiting
restriction $\overline1^vH_-^{-1}$ with $v\le m$, which is
annihilated in the same way.

These calculations remain valid when wall absorption or the
opening of an initial wall peak occurs at the same time.
Step~2 identifies the upper wall value retained in the
finite-product limit; any omitted part of that restriction
is supported on heights at most $m$ and is removed by the
displayed projections. Thus the two sides agree with the
prescribed right-time value of the kernel at $\tau=x_i$.

\smallskip\noindent
\emph{4. Trace-norm matching.}
On either regular side of $s_0$, Steps~1--3 identify the limit
of every grouped kernel entry with its value at $(\tau,g)$.
If there are simultaneous exceptional cases, expand a difference of finite
products by changing one factor at a time. 

All the entrywise limits have a common summable bound, since the original profile has a finite ceiling on $[0,B]$, and deterministic evolution cannot exceed that ceiling on
any of the dependence intervals under consideration. So Proposition~\ref{prop:trace-class} supplies a uniform
bound for the grouped, projected, weighted entries. Dominated convergence and
\eqref{eq:trace-by-entries} yield
\[
 \left\|
 \mathcal M J
 \bigl[K(\tau_s,g_s)-K(\tau,g)\bigr]\mathcal M
 \right\|_1
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
This proves \eqref{eqn:shiftcontinuity}.


\smallskip\noindent
\emph{5. Right continuity at a fixed profile.}
Fix $t>0$ and keep $h$ fixed. We first establish the
limits of the hitting kernels as the time parameter decreases
from $t+\varepsilon$ to $t$.

For any fixed $a>0$, local finiteness of the profile implies
that $h$ is constant with value $h(a^-)$ immediately to the
left of $a$. Similarly, for $b\ge0$, it is constant with
value $h(b^+)$ immediately to the right of $b$. Hence, for
all sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$,
\[
 Q_{a-\varepsilon,a}^h
 =Q_\varepsilon^{(h(a^-))}1_{h(a)},
 \qquad
 Q_{b,b+\varepsilon}^h
 =1_{h(b)}Q_\varepsilon^{(h(b^+))}.
\]
Upper semicontinuity gives
$h(a^-)\le h(a)$ and $h(b^+)\le h(b)$. Since \( \|Q_\varepsilon^{(m)}-1_m\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le e^{4\varepsilon}-1\), we obtain, in operator norm on $\ell^2(\mathbb Z)$,
\[
 Q_{a-\varepsilon,a}^h\to 1_{h(a)},
 \qquad
 Q_{b,b+\varepsilon}^h\to 1_{h(b)}.
\]
For $0<a\le b$, the constrained Markov property now gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 Q_{a-\varepsilon,b+\varepsilon}^h
 &=Q_{a-\varepsilon,a}^h
   Q_{a,b}^hQ_{b,b+\varepsilon}^h\to 
 1_{h(a)}Q_{a,b}^h1_{h(b)}
 =Q_{a,b}^h.
 \end{aligned}
\]
If the
left endpoint is zero, we have the similar convergence. Subtracting from the convergent free heat kernels yields \( P_{a-\varepsilon,b+\varepsilon}^h
 \to P_{a,b}^h,  P_{0,b+\varepsilon}^h
 \to P_{0,b}^h\).
These limits also cover collapsed intervals: \(a=b, b=0\) or \(a>b\).

Suppose first that $t\ne x_j$ for every $j$. For small
$\varepsilon$, the signs of \(W_{t+\epsilon\pm x_i,t+\epsilon\pm x_j}\) are fixed. The preceding calculations
therefore give its limit as the one in $K(t,h)$. If $t=x_j$, $t+\varepsilon-x_j>0$.
$P_{0,\varepsilon}^h\to\overline1^{h(0)}$, and all other
factors have the limits described above. A common upper bound for \(h\) on a
slightly enlarged dependence interval gives the same
summable bound. So using the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:trace-class} and dominated convergence, we have
\[
 \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}
 \widehat F_n(t+\varepsilon,h)=\widehat F_n(t,h).
\]
Here we do not assume \((t,h)\in \mathcal{R}_{\boldsymbol{x}}\).

Finally, the right-time limit at zero is
Proposition~\ref{thm:initial}. This proves \eqref{eqn:rightcontinuity}.

label: thm:verification-mild
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{thm:verification-mild}
For $0\le c<1$, the candidate $G$ is a bounded Borel solution of
the integral Kolmogorov equation~\eqref{eq:mild} on
$[0,T]\times\widehat{\mathcal X}_B$, with initial value $f$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The finite-product formulas and convergent Fredholm series make $G$
jointly Borel in $(t,h)$.
Propositions~\ref{thm:initial}
and~\ref{thm:uniform} give
\begin{equation}
 G(0,h)=f(h),\qquad |G(t,h)|\le C
       \quad(0\le t\le T+1,\ h\in\widehat{\mathcal X}_B).
\end{equation}
We first want to shift the trajectory so that it has finitely many exceptional times.
Fix $0<t\le T$, $h\in\widehat{\mathcal X}_B$, and $0<\varepsilon<1$. Define
\[ 
 h_s=\phi_s^B h,\qquad \tau_s=t+\varepsilon-s,\qquad
 v_\varepsilon(s)=G(\tau_s,h_s),\qquad 0\le s\le t.
\]
 The
deterministic semigroup property and \eqref{eq:deterministic-envelope} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:envelope-along-flow}
 r_0(\tau_s,x_j;\phi_s^B h)
 =r_0(t+\varepsilon,x_j;h).
\end{equation}
Hence all \((\tau_s,h_s)\) are allowed, or one fixed threshold is violated
throughout.

We choose $\varepsilon$ so that only finitely many times are
exceptional. Notice the condition that a step meets a hitting endpoint:
 \[
  z_i-\sigma_i s=(t-s)+x_j
  \qquad\text{or}\qquad
  z_i-\sigma_i s=|(t-s)-x_j|.
 \] 
Same sign on \(s\) will make \(s\) to be exception for a whole interval.
There are only finitely many such conditions on the total
time. Replacing $t$ by $t+\varepsilon$ and avoiding these intervals of exceptional time. The remaining exceptional times are finite in number.

Write $\mathcal L_{\rm det}=-\sum_i\sigma_i\partial_{y_i}$.
On an interval where \(v_{\epsilon}(s)\) is differentiable, Theorem~\ref{thm:classical} gives
\[
 v_\varepsilon'(s)
 =-\partial_\tau G(\tau_s,h_s)+\mathcal L_{\rm det}G(\tau_s,h_s)
 =(\mathcal L_{\rm det}-\mathcal L_c)G(\tau_s,h_s).
\]
Expanding the nucleation parts of the generator yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:shifted-trajectory-ode}
 \begin{split}
 v_\varepsilon'(s)
 &=-\int_{[0,B)}[G(\tau_s,C_zh_s)-G(\tau_s,h_s)]\,\mu_B(dz)\\
 &=\lambda_Bv_\varepsilon(s)
       -\int_{[0,B)}G(\tau_s,C_zh_s)\,\mu_B(dz).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Here $\mu_B([0,B))=\lambda_B$, including the wall atom $c\delta_0$.
If \((\tau_s,h_s)\notin \mathcal{A}_{\boldsymbol{r}}\), then also \((\tau_s,C_zh_s)\notin \mathcal{A}_{\boldsymbol{r}}\). Theorem~\ref{thm:FV}
then gives $G(\tau_s,h_s)=G(\tau_s,C_zh_s)=0$, so
\eqref{eq:shifted-trajectory-ode} holds on this curve as well.

On an allowed curve, Proposition~\ref{thm:transmission} matches the
regular pieces with the actual values at their endpoints, including
$s=0,t$. Bound~\eqref{eq:global-candidate-bound} gives
$|v_\varepsilon'|\le2\lambda_BC$ on each piece. Integrating this
bound, extending to endpoints by matching, and adding over the finite
partition show that $v_\varepsilon$ is Lipschitz on $[0,t]$.
On a forbidden curve it is identically zero. In both cases it is
absolutely continuous and satisfies \eqref{eq:shifted-trajectory-ode}
almost everywhere.

Multiplying \eqref{eq:shifted-trajectory-ode} by $e^{-\lambda_Bs}$ and integrating over \([0,t]\), we get
\begin{equation}\label{eq:shifted-integral-identity}
 \begin{split}
 G(t+\varepsilon,h)=e^{-\lambda_Bt}G(\varepsilon,\phi_t^B h)
 &+\int_0^t e^{-\lambda_Bs}
      \int_{[0,B)}G(t+\varepsilon-s,C_z\phi_s^B h)\,\mu_B(dz)\,ds.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Sending $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, Proposition~\ref{thm:transmission} and dominated convergence give \eqref{eq:mild}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $t>0$, a finite-valued initial profile $h$, and \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{r}\). Let $p_k$
be the probability of the height event with the usual bulk marks and
exactly $k$ independent uniform wall times in $[0,t]$, ordered in
time. These probabilities are independent of $c$ and lie in $[0,1]$.
Conditioning on the Poisson number of wall marks gives, for real $c\ge0$,
\[
 \mathbb P_h^c\bigl(h(t,x_j)\le r_j,\ 1\le j\le n\bigr)
       =e^{-ct}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(ct)^k}{k!}\,p_k.
\]
For complex $c$, the sum of absolute values is at most
$e^{t(|c|-\operatorname{Re}c)}$, uniformly on compact sets.
The right-hand side is therefore entire. 

The scalar Pfaffian is also entire in $c$. To see this,
fix $C_0<\infty$ and choose the weights in \eqref{eq:weights}
once for the disk $|c|\le C_0$. Write \(A(c):=\mathcal M J K(t,h;c)\mathcal M\).
The entries of $H_c$ and $H_-^{-1}$ are polynomials in $c$,
by \eqref{eq:H-kernel} and \eqref{eq:H-inverse-entries}, and the rest parts of kernel are independent of \(c\). The estimates in the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:trace-class} apply equally to complex
$c$ with $|c|\le C_0$, so every
entry of $A(c)$ is entire and the trace norm is uniformly bounded in \(c\). Thus, $\operatorname{Pf}(J+A(c))$ is entire. 

By Proposition~\ref{thm:verification-mild}, the two entire
functions agree for $0\le c<1$, so it gives \eqref{eq:multi-result} for every $c\ge0$ and $t>0$.

We now extend the identity to every $h\in\widehat{\mathcal X}$, allowing
the value $-\infty$. Fix $c\ge0$ and put
\[
 h^{(M)}:=h\vee(-M),\qquad M\in\mathbb N.
\]
These profiles are finite-valued and decrease to $h$.
Couple their evolutions with that from $h$ using the same
graphical marks, with the convention $-\infty+1=-\infty$.
Choose $B>x_n+t+1$, and let $N_B$ be the total number of
bulk and wall marks in $[0,t]\times[0,B]$. So,
\[
 h(t,x_j;h)
 \le h(t,x_j;h^{(M)})
 \le \max\{h(t,x_j;h),-M+N_B\}.
\]
Since $N_B<\infty$ almost surely, the height-event
indicators for $h^{(M)}$ and $h$ agree for all sufficiently
large $M$. Their probabilities therefore converge.

On the kernel side, for each $0\le a\le b\le B$ and
$u,v\in\mathbb Z$,
\[
 P_{a,b}^{h^{(M)}}(u,v)\downarrow P_{a,b}^h(u,v).
\]
 All the truncated profiles
have the common finite ceiling.
The same estimates in the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:trace-class} provide a common bound for the weighted kernel entries.
Dominated convergence and \eqref{eq:trace-by-entries}
therefore give
\[
 \left\|
 \mathcal M J
 \bigl(K(t,h^{(M)})-K(t,h)\bigr)\mathcal M
 \right\|_1\longrightarrow0.
\]


Finally, we extend it to \(t=0\). fix a real $c\ge0$ and take $B>x_n+1$. For $0<t<1$,
finite propagation and the event that there are no
nucleations in the dependence box give
\[
 \left|
 \mathbb P_h^c\bigl(h(t,x_j)\le r_j,\ 1\le j\le n\bigr)
 -f(\phi_t h)
 \right|
 \le 1-e^{-(2B+c)t}.
\]
Upper semicontinuity and the discreteness of the heights
imply that $f(\phi_t h)=f(h)$ for all sufficiently small $t$.
The transition probability therefore tends to $f(h)$ as
$t\downarrow0$. Taking this limit in the positive-time
identity proves that the prescribed right-time limiting
Pfaffian at $t=0$ equals $f(h)$, completing the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
For \(a\in \mathbb{R}\), \(e^{a\tau_{\pm}}(u,u\pm k) = \frac{a^k}{k!}, k>0\). Thus,
      \[\sum_{v}|e^{a\tau_{\pm}}(u,v)|e^{\lambda|u-v|}= \exp\{|a|e^{\lambda}\}.\]
We write \(S_{t,x}, e^{x\Delta}, L_{\pm}\) in terms of \(\tau_{\pm}\):
\[
 \begin{split}
 S_{t,x}=e^{-2x}e^{(x+t)\tau_+}e^{(x-t)\tau_-},\qquad e^{x\Delta}&=e^{-2x}e^{x\tau_+}e^{x\tau_-},\qquad
 L_\pm(t)=e^{2t}e^{-2t\tau_\pm}.
 \end{split}
\]
Thus, \(\sup_u\sum_v|D(u,v)|e^{\lambda|u-v|}\) is bounded respectively by
\[
 e^{2|x|+(|x+t|+|x-t|)e^\lambda},\qquad
 e^{2|x|+2|x|e^\lambda},\qquad
 e^{2|t|+2|t|e^\lambda}.
\]
Translation invariance gives the bounds on \(\sup_v\sum_u|D(u,v)|e^{\lambda|u-v|}\).

Let $N$ be the number of walk jumps on $[a,b]$. It is Poisson with
mean $2(b-a)\le2B$. A path from $u$ to $v$ that hits a profile
bounded above by $h_*$ must satisfy
\[
 N\ge(u-h_*)_++(v-h_*)_+,\qquad N\ge|u-v|.
\]
Let \(E = (u-h_*)_++(v-h_*)_++|u-v|\). Exponential Markov's inequality gives
\[P^{h}_{a,b}(u,v)\leq e^{-\lambda  E}\mathbb{E}(e^{2\lambda N})\leq e^{-\lambda E}\exp\{2B(e^{2\lambda}-1)\}.\]
For a terminal height at least $v$, replace the second lower
bound by $N\ge(v-u)_+$, and the same arguments hold.

label: eq:G-tail
title: Proof
body_md:
Recall the definition of \(G_{i,\pm}\) in \eqref{eq:G-exact}, \(L_{\pm}\) in \eqref{eq:Lpm}. We first establish the following two bounds: for every $\lambda>0$, uniformly on $|c|\le C_0$,
\begin{align}
 |G_{j,-}(z,v)|+|G_{j,+}(z,v)|&\le C_\lambda e^{-\lambda|z|-\lambda v},
 &&v>r_j,\label{eq:G-tail}\\
 |(L_+P_{a,b}^hL_-)(u,v)|+|(L_+P_{a,b}^hL_-H_-^{-1})(u,v)|
 &\le C_\lambda e^{-\lambda(u+v)},
 &&u>r_i,\ v>r_j,\label{eq:direct-tail}
\end{align}

Since \(L_-, L_-H^{-1}_-\) are uniformly bounded, we have \(|G(z,v)|\leq C \sum_{w\geq v}P_{0,s}^{h}(z,w)\). The exponent in
\eqref{eq:hit-cumulative} is at least $|z|+v-C'$:
for $z\ge0$, \((z-h_*)_++(v-h_*)_+>|z|+v-2h_*^+\); for $z<0$, $(v-z)_+\ge v+|z|$. 

For \eqref{eq:direct-tail}, the support and boundedness of the outer factors imply that it is bounded by $C\sum_{z\ge u,w\ge v}P_{a,b}^h(z,w)$.
Apply \eqref{eq:hit-tail} with exponent $2\lambda$,
\[\sum_{z\geq u,w\geq v}P_{a,b}^{h}(z,w)\leq C_\lambda e^{2\lambda h_*}(\sum_{z\geq u}e^{-\lambda z})(\sum_{w\geq v}e^{-\lambda w})\leq C_{\lambda,h_*} e^{-\lambda(u+v)}.\]

Now we bound the kernels in \eqref{eq:FG-terms} and \eqref{eq:positive-grouped}. There are three types of terms in \eqref{eq:FG-terms}: \(S G, (HS)^*G\) and \(G^*HG\). Choose $\lambda>\omega$, \eqref{eq:G-tail} gives
\[
 \begin{split}
      \sum_{z,w}|G_{i,\alpha}(z,u)H_c(z,w)G_{j,\beta}(w,v)|&\le C_\lambda e^{-\lambda(u+v)}\sum_{z,w}e^{-\lambda|z|}e^{\omega |z-w|}e^{-\lambda |w|}\\
 &\le C_\lambda e^{-\lambda(u+v)}
       \left(\sum_z e^{-(\lambda-\omega)|z|}\right)^2.
 \end{split}
\]
Using \eqref{eq:G-tail} and  \eqref{eq:free-tail},
\[|(S_{-t,-x_i}G_{j,\beta})(u,v)|\leq C_\lambda e^{-\lambda v}\sum_{z}|S(u,z)|e^{-\lambda|z|}\leq C_\lambda e^{-\lambda|u|-\lambda v}\le  C_\lambda e^{-\lambda(u+v)}.\]
Using \eqref{eq:G-tail} and \eqref{eq:H-free-growth},
\[ |((HS_{t,x_i})^*G_{j,\beta})(u,v)|
 \le C_\lambda e^{-\lambda v}
      \sum_z e^{\omega|z-u|-\lambda|z|}
 \le C_\lambda e^{\omega u-\lambda v}.\]
In the last inequality, $u>r_i$ permits replacing $|u|$ by $u$.
Taking adjoint handles the other terms. Hence, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scat-tail}
 |(J\widetilde K)_{ij}(u,v)|\le C_\lambda
 \begin{pmatrix}
 e^{-\lambda(u+v)}&e^{-\lambda u+\omega v}\\
 e^{\omega u-\lambda v}&e^{\omega u-\lambda v}+e^{-\lambda u+\omega v}
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad u>r_i,\ v>r_j.
\end{equation}

Choose $\lambda>\eta_n>\omega$ in \eqref{eq:scat-tail}. After the conjugation, \(\mathcal{M}(J\tilde{K})\mathcal{M}\) has all the exponents negative. 

It remains to consider the terms in \(R\). The $(+,+)$ component of $\mathcal{M}JR\mathcal{M}$ is 
\[
 e^{-\eta_i u-\eta_j v}|(e^{x_i\Delta}H_ce^{x_j\Delta})(u,v)|\leq Ce^{-\eta_i u-\eta_j v+\omega |u-v|}.
\]
Since \(u>r_i,v>r_j\), it is summable. For the free heat term with $i<j$, write
$q_d=e^{(x_j-x_i)\Delta}(0,d)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:free-heat-sum}
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{u>r_i,v>r_j}e^{\eta_i u-\eta_jv}|q_{v-u}|
 &=\sum_d|q_d|e^{-\eta_jd}
     \sum_{u>\max(r_i,r_j-d)}e^{-(\eta_j-\eta_i)u}\\
 &\le C\sum_d|q_d|e^{\eta_j|d|}<\infty.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
This is where the strict ordering of
$\eta_i$ is used.

The bound~\eqref{eq:trace-by-entries} now gives trace class with the
stated uniformity.

title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix the weights $\mathcal M$ and choose $B>x_n+t$. By regularity, there is a neighborhood $\mathcal U$ in the
time and step coordinates on which function heights on each constant interval,
the ordering of steps, hitting endpoints, and the regimes
in \eqref{eq:Wpq} remain unchanged. All profiles in this
neighborhood have a common finite ceiling $H$ on $[0,B]$.

\emph{Differentiability.}
Notice that the derivatives
are sums of translates of $P$ (terms from in \eqref{eq:endpoint-single}) and no-hit products forced
through neighboring heights at most $H+1$ (terms from \eqref{eqn:deterministicshift}). The jump-count argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:tails} therefore gives
\eqref{eq:hit-tail} and \eqref{eq:hit-cumulative} also for
the absolute values of these derivatives, with an enlarged
ceiling and constants, uniformly on $\mathcal U$.
Derivatives of \(S_{\pm t,\pm x}\) are finite sums of
translates and satisfy \eqref{eq:free-tail}; derivatives
of $L_\pm$ also retain their triangular support.

Apply the product rule to the grouped expressions
\eqref{eq:FG-terms}--\eqref{eq:positive-grouped}.
Using the same argument as in the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:trace-class}, we have
\[
 \sum_{i,j=1}^n\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in\{-,+\}}
 \sum_{u,v\in\mathbb Z}
 \sup_{\mathcal U}
 \bigl|D A_{ij}^{\alpha\beta}(u,v)\bigr|<\infty.
\]
The entrywise mean-value formula supplies the same summable
majorant for difference quotients. Dominated convergence,
together with \eqref{eq:trace-by-entries}, proves
differentiability in trace norm.

\emph{Integrability of nucleation increments.}
Put $\delta_zA=A(t,C_zh)-A(t,h)$.
Every hitting interval lies in $[0,x_n+t]$, so
$\delta_zA=0$ for $z>x_n+t$.
For $0\le z\le x_n+t$, the profiles $C_zh$ have the common
ceiling $H+1$. The estimates of
Proposition~\ref{prop:trace-class}, which do not depend on
the number or positions of the steps, consequently give
a common summable majorant for the entries of $\delta_zA$.

The finite-product representation \eqref{eq:plateau-product}, with the additional
restriction at $z$, shows that these entries are piecewise
continuous in $z$, with possible exceptions only at the
finitely many steps and hitting endpoints. We also have the bound
\[
 \int_0^\infty\|\delta_zA\|_1\,dz
 \le (x_n+t)\sup_{0\le z\le x_n+t}\|\delta_zA\|_1
 <\infty.
\]
Thus the increment is integrable in trace class.

label: lem:pfcalculus
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:pfcalculus}
Let $A$ be a skew trace-class kernel on $\mathcal H$. Let \(\Phi(A):=\operatorname{Pf}(J+A)\). Suppose $A=A(s)$ is differentiable in trace norm and \(I-JA(s)\) is invertible. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pf-derivative}
 \frac{d}{ds}\Phi(A(s))
 =
 -\frac12\Phi(A(s))
 \operatorname{tr}\!\left((I-JA(s))^{-1}J A'(s)\right).
\end{equation}
If $B$ is a skew rank-two operator and  \(I-JA(s)\) is invertible,
then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pf-affine}
 \Phi(A+B)-\Phi(A)
 =
 -\frac12\Phi(A)\operatorname{tr}\!\left((I-JA)^{-1}JB\right).
\end{equation}
If \(I-JA\) is not invertible, it is still true that
\[A'(s) =B \Rightarrow \frac{d}{ds}\Phi(A(s))= \Phi(A+B)-\Phi(A).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $I-JA(s)$ is invertible, \eqref{eq:pf-derivative} follows from the fact that \(\operatorname{Pf}^2(J+K)=\det(I-JK)\) and 
\[
 \frac{d}{ds}\det(I-JA(s))
 =
 -\det(I-JA(s))
 \operatorname{tr}\!\left((I-JA(s))^{-1}J A'(s)\right).
\]

To prove \eqref{eq:pf-affine}, assume \(B\) has the form \( B:=u\otimes v-v\otimes u\). Define the maps $U:\mathbb C^2\to\mathcal H$ and $V:\mathcal H\to\mathbb C^2$
by
\[
 U(a,b)=au+bv,\qquad
 Vf=\begin{pmatrix}v^{\mathsf T}f\\-u^{\mathsf T}f\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus, $B=UV$.

Since $I-JA$ is invertible, let
\[
 R=(J+A)^{-1}=-(I-JA)^{-1}J.
\]
Since $J+A$ is skew, $R^{\mathsf T}=-R$. Consequently,
\[
 u^{\mathsf T}Ru=v^{\mathsf T}Rv=0,
 \qquad
 u^{\mathsf T}Rv=-v^{\mathsf T}Ru.
\]
Writing $\alpha=v^{\mathsf T}Ru$, the determinant-square
identity and the finite-rank determinant identity give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Phi(A+B)^2
 &=\det(I-JA-JB)=\Phi(A)^2\det(I+RB)\\
 &=\Phi(A)^2\det(I+VRU)= \Phi(A)^2\det\begin{pmatrix}
  1+v^{\mathsf T}Ru & v^{\mathsf T}Rv\\
  -u^{\mathsf T}Ru & 1-u^{\mathsf T}Rv
 \end{pmatrix}\\
 &=
 \Phi(A)^2\det\begin{pmatrix}
  1+\alpha&0\\
  0&1+\alpha
 \end{pmatrix}
 =\Phi(A)^2(1+\alpha)^2.
 \end{aligned}
\]
So, \(\Phi(A+B)=\Phi(A)(1+\alpha)\). On the other hand, \(
 \operatorname{tr}(RB)
 =v^{\mathsf T}Ru-u^{\mathsf T}Rv
 =2\alpha\), so
\[
 \alpha
 =-\frac12\operatorname{tr}\!\left((I-JA)^{-1}JB\right).
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:pf-affine}.

When \(I-JA\) is not known to be invertible a prior, we use the Fr\'echet derivative; see \cite[Lemma 4.11]{MQR}.
